items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-turn text generators into long-running systems capable of multi-step reasoning, tool use, persistent memory, and reusable skill development. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve agent reliability, but existing approaches commonly treat verification as a fixed component of the reward structure, creating challenges related to sparse credit assignment, verifier reliability, reward hacking, path compliance, and verification cost. We introduce Budgeted Adaptive Verification with Asymmetric Rewards (BAVAR), a framework that formulates verification as a sequential, resource-constrained decision problem. BAVAR selectively determines what to verify, when verification is valuable, which verifier to invoke, and how verified evidence should influence learning based on uncertainty, action criticality, verifier reliability, expected verification value, and remaining computational budget. It combines reliability-gated positive process rewards with persistent penalties for path violations and extends verification to persistent memories and reusable skills. In an illustrative evaluation under matched verification budgets, BAVAR achieved 72.6% safe verified success, compared with 67.1% for uniform dense verification and 58.4% for outcome-only RLVR. Relative to dense verification, BAVAR reduced verification cost per safe success by 45.5% while using 47.8% fewer verifier tokens. It also reduced verified path violations to 7.2 per 100 trajectories, compared with 20.4 for outcome-only RLVR, and reduced successful verifier exploitation to 4.8%, compared with 15.9% for a single-judge baseline and 18.6% for outcome-only RLVR. For persistent artifacts, BAVAR achieved 88.7% held-out reuse success, compared with 81.3% for dense verification. These simulated findings suggest that adaptive allocation of verification resources can improve safe agent performance while reducing computational and verification overhead, providing a principled foundation for scalable verification of long-running autonomous agents.</jats:p>
title: Strategic Verification for Long-Running LLM Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) often generate fluent but incorrect or unsupported statements, commonly referred to as hallucinations. We propose a hallucination detection framework based on a Labeled Logic Program (LLP) architecture that integrates multiple reasoning paradigms, including logic programming, argumentation, probabilistic inference, and abductive explanation. By enriching symbolic rules with semantic, epistemic, and contextual labels and applying discourse-aware weighting, the system prioritizes nucleus claims over peripheral statements during verification. Experiments on three benchmark datasets and a challenging clinical narrative dataset show that LLP consistently outperforms classical symbolic validators, achieving the highest detection accuracy when combined with discourse modeling. A human evaluation further demonstrates that logic-assisted explanations improve both hallucination detection accuracy and user trust. The results suggest that labeled symbolic reasoning with discourse awareness provides a robust and interpretable approach to LLM verification in safety-critical domains.</jats:p>
title: From Argumentation to Labeled Logic Program for LLM Verification

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) can translate code between frameworks, languages and platform versions at a speed no human team can match, which makes them attractive for modernizing legacy software. Speed, however, shifts the bottleneck from writing code to trusting it. A migrated module that compiles and looks idiomatic may still change behavior in subtle ways, and legacy systems are precisely the systems least likely to have tests that would reveal such changes. This paper proposes a verification-first workflow in which behavioral evidence is established before any code is generated. The workflow has four gates: (1) capture current behavior with characterization tests; (2) generate the migration in small, reviewable units; (3) verify equivalence by differential testing of old and new implementations on the same inputs; and (4) review residual risk with a structured checklist that targets known LLM failure modes. We define a taxonomy of migration defects, metrics for migration trustworthiness, and an evaluation protocol. The workflow treats the LLM as a fast but fallible collaborator whose output is accepted only on evidence.</jats:p>
title: Trust but Verify: A Verification-First Workflow for LLM-Assisted Legacy Code Migration

items.abstract: <jats:p>When multiple large language models are consulted on the same question, agreement is often treated as evidence of reliability. That inference is weak when models share training data, development pipelines, or alignment methods, and a divergence-triggered procedure cannot address identical correlated errors. This paper isolates a narrower, tractable object: the procedural interval between visible inter-model divergence and final decision. We develop Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation (OMT), a low-machinery verification procedure. Models are queried separately, without access to one another's outputs and without debate, critique, or synthesis. Their divergences are preserved and classified before cross-exposure. A human observer selects decision-relevant divergences and routes each, by type, to grounding independent of the output chain under review. The verification chain ends with the return of grounding, not a synthesized verdict; final adoption is a separate, recorded human judgment. OMT retains five authorities on the human side: salience, routing, sufficiency, stopping, and final adoption. Each is assigned to a named decision-maker, with dispositions and stated grounds recorded. Cases with no observed divergence, or no selected divergence, close as screening prefixes and do not certify agreement. Because the observer is fallible, the method requires observation-condition logging and, in repeated deployment, an error-model ledger that includes both human and model failure modes. The paper defines the constitutive conditions, verification stages, provenance requirements, risk tiers, and failure modes of OMT. Four author-reported development episodes motivate the framework but do not validate it. OMT does not claim superiority over deliberation protocols or improved decision accuracy. Its designed contribution is narrower: to make the path from divergence to external grounding, and from grounding to adoption, attributable and inspectable.</jats:p>
title: Observer-Mediated Multi-LLM Triangulation: Human-Routed External Verification Without Inter-Model Deliberation

items.abstract: <jats:p>High code coverage does not guarantee complete verification. Coverage metrics measure where tests exercise the design, but not whether outputs are actually checked. This gap between exercising code and validating results-the verification gap-allows bugs to escape even with 99%+ coverage. When outputs differ between correct and faulty RTL, but all tests still pass, checkers are missing. This paper presents a novel methodology for identifying verification gaps through LLM-aided analysis of mutation-induced behavioral divergence. The approach combines automated fault injection with structured LLM prompting to systematically detect missing checkers that coverage metrics cannot reveal. The theoretical foundation rests upon a constructive proof: injection of semantically non-equivalent mutations into golden RTL, followed by differential simulation, exposes precisely those output behaviors that evade checker scrutiny. The workflow is straightforward: (i) introduce a small change (mutation) to the RTL, (ii) run the same tests on both original and mutated versions, (iii) if outputs differ but tests pass, a gap exists, (iv) use an LLM to suggest the missing checker, and (v) validate the fix. The entire detection cycle takes about 80 seconds per mutation. Proof-of-concept validation on two representative IP blocks-a round-robin arbiter (350 LOC, algorithmic complexity) and synchronous FIFO (150 LOC, numeric boundaries)-demonstrates methodology feasibility: 4× time reduction, 100% precision (zero false positives), and cross-domain applicability across distinct fault morphologies. Break-even analysis yields N * ≈ 10 faults for initial deployment with asymptotic reduction to N * ≈ 2 upon amortization. The results establish feasibility of LLM-aided gap detection as a complement to traditional coverage-driven verification.</jats:p>
title: LLM-Aided Verification Gap Detection: A Methodology for Identifying Missing Checkers in UVM Testbenches

items.abstract: We address LLM serving workloads where repeated requests share a common solution structure but differ in localized constraints such as output schema, variable names, or numeric constants. Prior caching approaches typically reuse either full responses (semantic caching) or model-internal KV/prefix states, which are brittle under partial changes or tightly coupled to specific backends. We present StepCache , a backend-agnostic step-level reuse layer that segments outputs into ordered steps, retrieves the best matching cached request, verifies steps using lightweight task-aware checks, and regenerates only failing regions through selective patching. StepCache also supports strict structured-output enforcement for JSON through single-step extraction, required-key constraints, and one-shot repair, and includes conservative skip-reuse fallbacks for semantic changes. For linear equations, StepCache promotes verification into correction via a bounded repair loop with a deterministic fallback that guarantees correctness when the backend model fails. In a CPU-only perturbation-heavy micro-benchmark on math and JSON variants (10 base prompts per task with 3 variants per perturbation, totaling 222 evaluation requests per seed), averaged over three seeds (42–44), StepCache reduces mean latency from 2.13 seconds to 0.67 seconds (median: 2.42 seconds to 0.01 seconds; p95: 3.38 seconds to 3.30 seconds), reduces total token usage from 36.1k to 27.3k (162.7 to 123 tokens per request), and improves end-to-end correctness from 72.5% to 100% under both task-specific checks and a stitched-output integrity check. Across requests, 79.7% take the reuse-only fast path, 5.4% require patching, and 14.9% trigger skip-reuse.
title: StepCache: Step-Level Reuse with Lightweight Verification and Selective Patching for LLM Serving

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid proliferation of sophisticated large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized content generation but concurrently poses significant challenges for distinguishing human-authored from AI-generated text. Traditional detection methods often struggle with the increasing fluency of LLM outputs and their vulnerability to adversarial manipulations. In response, we propose LLM-as-Critic, a novel discriminative framework that fine-tunes a pre-trained LLM to act as an expert judge of textual authenticity. Our method integrates a multi-objective training paradigm encompassing Binary Cross-Entropy loss for fundamental classification, a bespoke Contrastive Learning loss to maximize inter-class separation, and an Adversarial Training scheme to bolster robustness against sophisticated AI-generated content. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets, including news, creative writing, and academic papers, consistently demonstrate LLM-as-Critic's superior performance, achieving F1 scores up to 0.97, significantly outperforming baselines such as Perplexity-based Detectors, Stylometric Feature Analyzers, and Fine-tuned RoBERTa Classifiers. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the incremental contribution of each training component, while human evaluation confirms a higher agreement rate with our model's classifications, reinforcing its practical utility. LLM-as-Critic establishes a new state-of-the-art in AI-generated text detection, particularly excelling in generalization to unseen generators and resilience against adversarial attacks.</jats:p>
title: LLM-as-Critic: Contrastive and Adversarial Strategies for Authentic Text Verification

items.abstract:
<jats:p>We describe DAI (Decripte Artificial Intelligence), a deployed system in which a software agent conducts an incident-response episode end to end — curating a signal, extracting a target from structured evidence, selecting a reviewed playbook, emitting an action contract, having that contract adjudicated by a decision function that is pure in its declared inputs, executing at a network edge, verifying through a credential provably incapable of writing, sealing a hash-linked transcript, and returning on a schedule to review, reconcile, and undo — with no human approving any step. 
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 The system’s contributions as an artifact are: (i) a decision function δ(a, λ, h) whose domain excludes every learned output, making independence from the model a consequence of the signature rather than of a runtime check; (ii) separation of duties realized as capability disjointness between two credentials, verified empirically against the enforcement provider’s API before deployment — the verifying credential receives an authentication error when it attempts to write; (iii) a receipt satisfying a recomputation contract, recomputed in production by a verifier importing none of the system’s code, with exact tamper localization demonstrated by controlled alteration; (iv) per-principal perimeters inside a shared enforcement domain, requiring containment predicates that conjoin a hostname discriminator with the source address, and an aggregation scheme that multiplies simultaneous-containment capacity by the expression-length limit under a platform rule budget; (v) an element-identified reconciliation algorithm that remains sound under that aggregation, where the conventional rule-identified algorithm is unsound in both directions; and (vi) a domain language model trained exclusively on the system’s own outcome-verified transcripts, which narrates and is structurally incapable of deciding.
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 We report production measurements: a containment executed, verified by a distinct credential, and sealed 887 ms after the episode’s first turn, including two round trips to the enforcement provider; a receipt of twelve turns recomputed externally with all links valid and, under single-character alteration of turn zero, failing at exactly the altered index; zero-blast-radius isolation confirmed by the absence of any domain-wide rule for the contained address; and the full testimony→review→undo cycle closing. We also report ten defects found in the period, every one of which was silent, and analyse what each revealed.
</div></jats:p>
title: DAI: A Domain-Specific LLM with Model-Excluded Authority, Capability-Disjoint Verification, and Recomputable Receipts

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now used in procedural guidance and decision-making in legal information services and in public-sector administrative systems, not only to supplement human judgment but also to serve as a replacement for it. These systems, even though they seem fluent, are also likely to engage in hallucination, which is the creation of appropriate and convincing content not backed up by facts. Hallucination within the framework of the public sector is not only a technical flaw but a risk of governance and operation because erroneous procedural guidance or misleading legal foundations can weaken the legal certitude, administrative responsibility, and civic trust. The previous literature on hallucination detection has mainly been model-based or grounded on retrieval methods, unlikely to do well in practical limits of deployment such as black-box LLM APIs and fewer retraining options. This paper suggests a risk-based verification and validation (V&V) model that redefines the problem of hallucination processing as a governance issue and not an accuracy-focused activity. The model proposes a slot-based separation in line with the administrative methodology and it incorporates cross sample instability, coverage of citation and rule based validation into a composite Hallucination Risk Index. Examples of quantitative risk indicators transformed into operational decisions, such as conditional response, or deferral or escalation to human officers, are illustrative examples of situations in the public sector. The suggested framework puts hallucination management in line with the conventional wisdom of system and software assurance by integrating the hallucination evaluation into the ISO/IEC-style verification and validation artefacts, which offers a viable and verifiable course of action towards responsible use of the LLM-based systems in government administration.
title: A Risk-Oriented Verification and Validation Framework for Hallucination Detection in Public-Sector LLM Systems

items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 When a pipeline's output carries legal weight, a verifier that reads an implementer's claims and reasons about them produces an opinion. What a compliance record requires is primary execution evidence produced independently of those claims. This paper presents a dual-agent coordination protocol in which the verifying agent re-executes the production pipeline directly, before reading the implementing agent's self-verification results, and posts its findings as first-hand evidence with file-and-line citations to the live codebase. We call this ratification to distinguish it from review, critique, scoring, and debate. Ratification is the act of confirming a claim through independent re-execution of the system the claim describes, not through reasoning about the claim itself.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;The protocol is mediated by two directional append-only outbox files on a shared filesystem. Each file has exactly one writer. A filesystem watcher fires on each file when new content is appended, waking the opposing agent without polling. Neither agent can modify what the other has written. Retraction is public, timestamped, and permanent. The outbox files serve simultaneously as coordination channel, audit trail, and session memory across sessions measured in days.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; We demonstrate the protocol in a multi-week production session on a candidate screening system operating under EU AI Act Article 9 risk management, Article 13 transparency, and Article 15 accuracy and robustness requirements. In a two-hour sample window spanning 237 coordination cycles, the protocol surfaces twelve distinct defect classes with zero regressions across a monotonically growing test suite reaching 4,851 passing tests. Eight defects originate in the implementing agent's work and are caught by the verifying agent's independent re-execution. Four originate in the verifying agent's own output and are caught by the same mechanism applied symmetrically. The execution asymmetry between the two agents, one orchestrating multi-phase parallel subagent workflows and the other executing the production chain directly without orchestration, is the structural condition that makes genuine independence possible and that distinguishes this protocol from all prior multi-agent verification approaches. To our knowledge, no prior work demonstrates a dual-agent verification protocol sustaining zero regressions across a session of this duration in a legally consequential production pipeline.
</div></jats:p>
title: Ratification by Re-execution: A Dual-agent Protocol for Independent Verification in Legally Consequential LLM Pipelines

items.abstract: <jats:p>Objective. Token-level confidence estimates from large language models (LLMs) do not reflect whether a generated clinical summary is factually correct. We investigate whether verification-based confidence prediction improves upon token-level estimates and whether LLM-as-judge labels can be assumed reliable for clinical summarization evaluation. Methods. Using MIMIC-IV, we construct 500 clinical summarization tasks across four open-source LLMs (Qwen2.5-14B/32B, Phi-4, Llama-3.1-8B), producing 2,000 primary summaries and 1,500 self-consistency samples. Each summary is scored on 26 verification features spanning coverage, factual consistency, natural language inference, numerical accuracy, semantic similarity, and self-consistency. Ground-truth labels are generated by Codex-GPT-5 and validated by two board-certified physicians on 200 summaries. Results. Three judges produce markedly different label distributions (Codex-GPT-5: 93.4% problematic, Phi-4: 10.5%, physicians: 59.5%) with near-zero pairwise agreement ($\kappa = 0.009$–$0.151$). Each physician independently identified only 1 of 200 summaries as fully trustworthy. ClinTrust achieves AUROC = 0.846 [95% CI: 0.788, 0.896] against Codex-GPT-5 labels and 0.695 [0.619, 0.768] against physician labels, significantly outperforming single-feature baselines including token log-probability (0.583) and BERTScore-F1 (0.607). Conclusions. Multi-source verification improves upon token-level confidence for predicting summary reliability, but LLM-as-judge labels are highly variable and cannot be assumed reliable without human validation.</jats:p>
title: Confidence Is Not Probability: Verification-Based Confidence Prediction for LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries

items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 LLM agents deployed in financial environments must produce outputs that are verifiably correct. Existing benchmarks focus on knowledge retrieval, sentiment analysis, or arithmetic on isolated questions, and do not evaluate the forensic reasoning required to audit large structured datasets across disjointed schemas.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 We introduce two contributions. First, the Pave Interchange Fee Benchmark, a 24-task evaluation suite spanning four levels of forensic complexity, requiring agents to perform multi-file reconciliation, systematic error detection, and financial impact modelling on a synthetic dataset of 50,000 transaction records modelled after real payment processor settlement data. Second, the Adversarial Verification Architecture (Avae 2.0), a three-role multi-agent system in which an Auditor, an Adversarial Verifier, and a Consensus Judge collaborate through a structured rebuttal protocol.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 We evaluate Avae 2.0 against eight state-of-the-art single-agent baselines. Single-agent models perform reasonably on Level 1 aggregation tasks but degrade sharply on Level 3 forensic discovery, with accuracy falling below 55% across all baselines. Avae 2.0 achieves 100% accuracy across all four task levels. We attribute single-agent failure to three recurring patterns: relational blindness, numerical drift, and contextual overload. Our results suggest that architectural constraints, specifically the adversarial consensus requirement, are an important factor in reliability on structured financial reasoning tasks, independent of model scale. The benchmark dataset, evaluation scripts, and ground truth answers are publicly available at github.com/avae-ai/pave-benchmark.
</div></jats:p>
title: Adversarial Consensus Verification for Reliable LLM agents in Financial Forensics: The Pave Interchange Benchmark

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in industrial monitoring and decision support, yet they remain prone to process-control hallucinations—diagnoses and explanations that sound plausible but conflict with physical constraints, sensor data, or plant dynamics. This paper investigates hallucination as a failure of abductive reasoning, where missing premises, weak mechanistic support, or counter-evidence lead an LLM to propose incorrect causal narratives for faults such as pump restriction, valve stiction, fouling, or reactor runaway. We develop a neuro-symbolic framework in which Abductive Logic Programming (ALP) evaluates the coherence of model-generated explanations, counter-abduction generates rival hypotheses that test whether the explanation can be defeated, and Discourse-weighted ALP (D-ALP) incorporates nucleus–satellite structure from operator notes and alarm logs to weight competing explanations. Using our 500-scenario Process-Control Hallucination Dataset, we assess LLM reasoning across mechanistic, evidential, and contrastive dimensions. Results show that abductive and counter-abductive operators substantially reduce explanation-level hallucinations and improve alignment with physical process behavior, particularly in “easy-but-wrong’’ cases where a superficially attractive explanation contradicts historian trends or counter-evidence. These findings demonstrate that abductive reasoning provides a practical and verifiable foundation for improving LLM reliability in safety-critical process-control environments.</jats:p>
title: Neuro-Symbolic Verification for Preventing LLM Hallucinations in Process Control

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on multi-step reasoning and analogical transfer (often across domains), yet current practices often lack explicit governance, auditability, and structured verification. This paper introduces the Structural Alignment and Verification Protocol (SAVP), a protocollevel governance framework that decomposes reasoning into four inspectable stages: structure extraction, alignment proposal, solution synthesis, and verification. SAVP emphasizes explicit intermediate artifacts-alignment mappings and verification traces-that enable structured auditing, ablation, and reproducible evaluation. Prompt examples are illustrative only; the contribution is the protocol and auditable artifacts. SAVP is positioned as an auditable verification layer for LLM reasoning systems, situated at the intersection of artificial intelligence methodology and evaluation design. While motivated by analogical reasoning, the protocol generalises to broader structured reasoning and verification scenarios. This staged release focuses on protocol specification, trace schema design, and an evaluation blueprint, including the Distal Analogy Suite (DAS) for controlled distal cross-domain testing. Prompt examples and pilot traces are provided solely as illustrative realizations of the protocol and should not be interpreted as normative prompting recipes. The current version does not claim empirical performance improvements; full benchmarking and large-scale ablations are reserved for subsequent revisions. This paper provides a protocol specification and pilot results to validate the artifact pipeline, with full benchmarking deferred. This paper argues that treating reasoning workflows as protocol-governed processes-with explicit verification artifacts-offers a practical pathway toward more transparent and auditable LLM reasoning research.</jats:p>
title: From Structural Alignment to Verification Governance: A Protocol for Auditable LLM Reasoning Protocol Specification and Evaluation Blueprint

items.abstract: <jats:p>As Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional capabilities in code generation, their application within the Hardware Description Language (HDL) design flow has become a focal point for both academia and industry. However, compared to the software domain, hardware design imposes far more stringent requirements on correctness. The potential stochastic defects in LLM-generated code pose substantial challenges for backend verification, leading to what we term an "Efficiency Paradox": accelerated front-end generation paired with decelerated back-end verification. Reported figures across the surveyed literature suggest that the first-pass functional correctness of code generated by monolithic models is frequently below 60% on standard benchmarks, with verification convergence cycles growing non-linearly with design complexity. To clarify the development status and challenges in this field, this study conducted a Systematic Mapping Study (SMS) of peer-reviewed literature on LLMs applied to Register Transfer Level (RTL) design published between January 2020 and January 2026 (with the primary high-quality corpus concentrated in 2023–2025, reflecting the period of rapid growth in this field). The initial search yielded 1,245 records. After deduplication and title/abstract screening, 107 papers entered full-text eligibility assessment. Using the exclusion criteria (EC1–EC7) we excluded 41 papers, and a subsequent Empirical Rigor Score (ERS) screening with threshold ERS≥1.0 excluded a further 4 early papers that lacked quantitative data or relied solely on ”toy examples,” for a combined 45 exclusions and a final corpus of 62 included primary studies. Analysis of these 62 studies indicates that the field is undergoing a paradigm shift from early ”one-shot syntactic generation” toward ”verification-centric, agent-based collaborative systems.” This study establishes a four-stage verification paradigm taxonomy, identifies distinctive defect categories associated with LLM-generated RTL (syntax hallucination, logical inconsistency, and semantic injection/security vulnerabilities), and critically examines the limitations of current evaluation metrics. Several scope limitations apply: the corpus is dominated by Verilog/SystemVerilog studies; FPGA-level validation is reported in only 11% of included studies; and cross-phase Pass@1 comparisons pool heterogeneous benchmarks and should be read as indicative trends rather than controlled comparisons. The results aim to provide a structured technical roadmap for researchers and EDA practitioners, guiding future construction of more reliable, intelligent chip design flows that incorporate self-healing capabilities.</jats:p>
title: Bridging the Efficiency Paradox: A Systematic Mapping Study on Verification Paradigms in LLM-Generated RTL

items.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems improve reasoning reliability by letting several agents solve a task and reconciling their answers through debate or voting, often followed by a verification stage that checks intermediate steps with additional judges or tools. These pipelines assume that agents and verifiers err independently. In practice, agents from the same model family share training data and failure modes, so their verdicts are correlated and repeated same-family checks carry far less evidence than independence suggests. This paper treats verification as a resource-allocation problem under correlated errors and proposes CAVEAT (Correlation-Aware VErification AllocaTion). CAVEAT merges heterogeneous agent traces into a claim dependency graph, models each verifier by Beta-distributed sensitivity and specificity together with a family-level shared-slip rate that yields a closed-form correlated posterior, and greedily selects which claim to verify, by which verifier and when to stop by a cost-normalised value of information. Ignoring correlation inflates posterior log-odds by a design-effect factor 1+(k−1)ρ, and the greedy policy is near-optimal under adaptive submodularity. On six public benchmarks covering claim verification, multi-hop question answering and mathematical reasoning, with eight heterogeneous verifiers, CAVEAT matches exhaustive verification at 21% of its cost, improves accuracy over the strongest budget-matched baseline by 3.1 points, reduces expected calibration error from 7.4% to 3.8% and lowers the rate of confidently accepted wrong answers from 19.6% to 7.2%.
title: CAVEAT: Reliability-aware active verification under correlated errors for multi-agent LLM reasoning

items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent advances in care robots for older adults have improved assistive monitoring, activity recognition, and human-robot interaction; however, most existing approaches remain perception-centric and lack integrated privacy modeling, real-time reasoning within the control loop, and adaptive alignment with user preferences, consent requirements, and contextual needs. In addition, emerging capabilities such as emotion recognition and LLM-based interaction introduce inferencedriven privacy risks that are insufficiently addressed in current frameworks. This paper proposes CAREAssist, a privacyaware and context-adaptive care robot framework that embeds privacy and safety into a closed-loop perception-reasoningverification-action pipeline by combining multi-modal perception with LLM-based contextual reasoning. It introduces a real-time privacy risk engine that quantifies data sensitivity, identity exposure, and inference risks, alongside a policydriven verification module that enforces privacy and safety constraints before action execution. The framework further adapts robot behavior according to user trust and preferences, and experimental results in simulated care environments demonstrate improved task performance, reduced privacy risks, and enhanced alignment with user preferences.</jats:p>
title: CAREAssist: A Privacy-Aware Context-Adaptive Care Robot for Older Adults Using Perception-LLM-Verification Loop

items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for C++ code generation, yet their ability to satisfy Motor Industry Software Reliability Association (MISRA) C++:2023 guidelines at scale remains unclear. This study conducts a controlled before–after, repeated-measures study on 26 C++ tasks, evaluating four models with 20 runs per condition. Compiled outputs are checked with a complete MISRA C++:2023 ruleset. Verbose rule texts are distilled into compact, actionable Top-k instruction packs (k=3,5,10) targeting each model’s most frequent violations. Primary outcomes are violations per thousand lines of code (KLOC), compile rate, and pass rate. At baseline, models cluster at 23–29 violations/KLOC, dominated by an advisory rule discouraging standard integer type names. Adding Top-k instructions reduces violations by 44–83% across models (paired permutation tests, all p < 0.01); GPT-5 and o3 reach 3.9–4.5 violations/KLOC. Functional impacts are small overall; two conditions show significant pass-rate declines (GPT-4.1/Top-3, o3/Top-10). Improvements spill over to non-targeted rules. Compact, model-aware MISRA prompts therefore offer a practical path to safer C++ generation with limited functional cost when scoped appropriately. However, full verification still requires dedicated compliance tooling to detect residual issues, quantify results for certification, and produce auditable evidence for regulators. Practitioners should adopt a step-up strategy, start with Top-3 or Top-5 rules, monitor compile and pass rates, and expand only when stable. Study artifacts are released to enable replication and reuse.
title: Reducing MISRA violations in LLM-generated code by 83%: An empirical study with static analysis verification

items.abstract: Background: A guarded language-model pipeline can select a clinical calculator, extract inputs, execute deterministic code, and check whether an alternate representation returns the same value. Such agreement may verify arithmetic execution without establishing that the selected calculator fits the case. Objective: To test whether CIBB-Guard's internal consistency check can pass after an inappropriate calculator choice and to compare the guarded configuration with direct prompting. Methods: One frozen local Llama 3.1 8B model was evaluated on a prespecified 1,043-record benchmark and, post hoc, on 77 human-adjudicated de-identified case reports classified as eligible or ineligible for the evaluated calculators. Results: On 33 ineligible cases, CIBB-Guard correctly declined 21 but accepted 12 inappropriate answers; 11 of those 12 passed genuine alternate-representation re-verification. On 44 eligible cases, it produced 4 correct answers versus 0 with direct prompting. On the benchmark, all-record correctness was 631/1,043 (60.5%) for CIBB-Guard and 101/1,043 (9.7%) for direct prompting; all accepted confirmatory answers were synthetic. Conclusions: Internal execution consistency does not establish calculator applicability. This one-model benchmark and case-series study supports separate applicability checks and does not establish clinical safety or deployment readiness.
title: When Verification Passes the Wrong Calculator: A Human-Adjudicated Study of a Guarded Local LLM Pipeline

items.abstract: <jats:p>Planning in robotics represents an ongoing research challenge, as it requires the integration of sensing, reasoning, and execution. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a high degree of flexibility in planning, they often introduce hallucinated goals and actions and consequently lack the formal reliability of deterministic methods. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a hybrid Sense–Plan–Code–Act (SPCA) framework that combines perception, LLM-based reasoning, and symbolic planning. Within the proposed approach, sensory information is first transformed into a symbolic description of the world in Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) using an LLM. A heuristic planner is then used to generate a valid plan, which is subsequently converted to code by a second LLM. The generated code is first validated syntactically through compilation and then semantically in simulation. When errors are detected, local corrections can be applied and the process is repeated as necessary. The proposed method is evaluated in the OpenAI Gym MiniGrid reinforcement learning environment and in a Gazebo simulation on a UR5 robotic arm using a curriculum of tasks with increasing complexity. The system successfully completes approximately 71–75% of tasks across environments with a relatively low number of simulation iterations.</jats:p>
title: Robot Planning via LLM Proposals and Symbolic Verification

                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study was to test three prompts instructing an Artificial Intelligence large language model to determine if citations were correct to see which was the most effective. Another purpose was to analyze the prompts’ quality using the concise, logical, explicit, adaptive and reflective (CLEAR) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>45 altered citations from 15 American Psychologist citations were tested across three prompt strategies (Verify, Correct and Fit), resulting in 135 prompts to Microsoft CoPilot. A quantitative chi-square analysis and the CLEAR framework were used to analyze the results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Fit prompt (“find the closest fitting citation for”) was the most effective at providing correct citations. Only the Fit prompt was concise, logical, explicit, adaptive and reflective. The Correct prompt “‘amend the citation to be factually accurate”) provoked some “corrective hallucinations,” where CoPilot hallucinated incorrect citations in providing corrections to the altered citations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no one has developed a prompt similar to the “Fit” prompt. This prompt, although not perfect, has some practical value for identifying incorrect citations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Think like an LLM: testing three AI citation verification prompts

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that autonomously execute tool calls for users are increasingly deployed in customer-facing settings, where peer-based trust and reputation mechanisms — long used in multi-agent systems to infer trustworthiness from peer testimony — are natural candidates for calibrating confidence in an agent’s self-report. Yet whether such peer testimony can detect when an agent’s self-report is unfaithful to verified ground truth has not been empirically examined using real production data. This paper studies 1,980 real agent trajectories from tau-bench, spanning two domains (retail, airline) and two production models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet), each verified against ground-truth database-state comparisons. Self-reported success claims are unfaithful to verified outcomes in 13.8 to 31.5 percent of trajectories, with false-success more common than false-failure. Whether cross-agent peer verification — including reputation-weighted aggregation, the canonical multi-agent trust-inference mechanism — transfers from prior shared-observation settings to this independent-execution setting is then tested; it does not, since trials are independent stochastic re-attempts rather than shared-event observations, with all four aggregation rules underperforming solo self-report (56.5 percent versus 51.7–55.6 percent). This difference is statistically significant (Holm–Bonferroni corrected) against naive-mean and reputation-weighted aggregation in both peer-group compositions and against trimmed mean in the pooled-model setting, and is distinct from a separate failure mode driven by correlated errors rather than absent shared observation. Motivated by this result, a calibration strategy using peer task-difficulty quartiles is proposed, distinguishing its oracle-level from its realistically-deployable effectiveness. The rule-based classifier used throughout is validated against constructed edge cases and 152 messages sampled from the real corpus, yielding 88.2% agreement and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.812. As a preliminary domain-generalization check, the same pipeline is applied to 43 newly collected trajectories from the telecom domain of τ²-bench (tau-bench’s successor); results are directionally consistent but, based on a single model and much smaller sample, are reported as a non-confirmatory pilot rather than a full replication. This work identifies a structural boundary condition on when peer-based trust and reputation mechanisms are informative in multi-agent systems — showing that they transfer from shared-observation domains to independent-execution agentic settings only partially, and characterizing empirically when and why.
title: When Does Cross-Agent Peer Verification Detect Unfaithful Self- Reports? An Empirical Study of Real LLM Tool-Use Agent Trajectories

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) often generate fluent but
in-correct or unsupported statements, commonly referred to
as hallucinations. We propose a hallucination detection
frame-work based on a Labeled Logic Program (LLP)
architecture that integrates multiple reasoning paradigms,
including logic programming, argumentation, probabilistic
inference, and ab-ductive explanation. By enriching
symbolic rules with seman-tic, epistemic, and contextual
labels and applying discourse-aware weighting, the system
prioritizes nucleus claims over peripheral statements
during verification. Experiments on three benchmark
datasets and a challenging clinical narrative dataset show
that LLP consistently outperforms classical symbolic
validators, achieving the highest detection accuracy when
combined with discourse modeling. A human evaluation
further demonstrates that logic-assisted explanations
im-prove both hallucination detection accuracy and user
trust. The results suggest that labeled symbolic reasoning
with dis-course awareness provides a robust and
interpretable ap-proach to LLM verification in
safety-critical domains.</jats:p>
title: From Argumentation to Labeled Logic Program for LLM Verification

items.abstract: <jats:p>Modern power system simulation workflows, including model setup, parameter configuration, scenario construction, solver invocation, and result verification, remain heavily manual and procedurally intensive. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to transform high-level engineering intents into structured and reviewable simulation workflows. Yet, as probabilistic models, LLMs may generate outputs that are incomplete, incorrectly ordered, or inconsistent with the active simulation state, posing risks to workflow reliability. This paper proposes a trustworthy intent-driven LLM-agent workflow with state verification for power system simulation. The proposed framework separates LLM-based workflow planning from solver-side execution. The LLM converts heterogeneous engineering instructions into structured and reviewable candidate workflows, while a state-verification mechanism checks workflow admissibility, state-dependency constraints, and execution evidence before solver-side results are accepted. Instead of evaluating only software executability, the proposed evaluation distinguishes planning validity from verified workflow completion, where a workflow is successful only when the executed workflow satisfies the required state conditions of the intended simulation task. A controlled benchmark on the New England 39-bus system evaluates robustness under different task-complexity levels and instruction-ambiguity variants, with ablation studies quantifying the roles of schema guidance, orchestration, and LLM backbone selection. A real-world 201-bus power system further assesses practical scalability in model preparation and N-1 contingency testing. Results show that the proposed workflow reduces low-level manual interaction, achieving approximately a 19-fold improvement in model-preparation workflow efficiency and a 4.5-fold speedup in N-1 contingency-test workflow execution.</jats:p>
title: A Trustworthy Intent-Driven LLM-Agent Workflow with State Verification for Power System Simulation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models are increasingly used for structured knowledge verification, where reliable knowledge verification is essential for identifying potentially incorrect predictions. Existing disagreement-based uncertainty methods assume that repeated outputspreserve observable variation. However, semantically plausible false claims may produce unanimous but incorrect predictions, causing disagreement observability collapse before uncertainty computation. On a controlled stress test, SC-3 has Zero-Entropy Ratesof 83.9% on deceptive examples and 76.5% on 1,491 aligned examples. Its Wrong-Unanimity Rate (WUR) is 67.5% (326/483 errors). As a diagnostic intervention, Multi-View Conflict Aggregation (MVCA) decomposes verification into factual, semantic,and structural dimensions rather than introducing arbitrary prompt diversity. MVCA reduces the corresponding Zero-Entropy Rates to 39.1% and 55.9% and has a WUR of 39.1% (175/448 errors). It obtains AURC 0.234 with three calls, compared with 0.231 for 20 homogeneous samples. The benefit reverses on weaker backbones that do not respond differently to the assigned dimensions. Reliable LLM-based knowledge verification depends on whether diagnostically useful disagreement remains observable before uncertainty aggregation. Task-aligned verification decomposition helps only when the backbone can distinguish the relevant verification dimensions.</jats:p>
title: Diagnosing Disagreement Observability Collapse in LLM-based Structured KnowledgeVerification: Restoring Uncertainty Signals through Task-Aligned Multi-View Verification

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in generating human-like text, yet their outputs often suffer from critical issues such as hallucination, ethical violations, and lack of meaningfulness. These challenges can result in misinformation, offensive language, and unreliable outputs, especially in niche languages like Turkish. To address these concerns, we introduce KorvexChecker, a modular and multi-functional tool for validating LLM outputs in terms of ethical compliance, meaningfulness, and hallucination detection. KorvexChecker employs a combination of fine-tuned BERT models for sentiment analysis, ethical violation detection, and text classification to identify whether a given text requires further verification. The tool integrates various external verification resources, such as Web Search API for factual accuracy and journal database for academical document validation. Furthermore, Zemberek, a Turkish NLP library, is utilized for preprocessing, normalization, and segmentation of Turkish text. The system was evaluated on a custom-labeled dataset of 7552 Turkish samples, divided into training, validation, and test sets. Experimental results demonstrate that the BERT-based classifiers achieved an average F1-score of 93.3% across multiple tasks, significantly outperforming both rule-based methods and traditional machine learning baselines. A small-scale user test showed the framework to be responsive and effective in real-time scenarios, with an average inference latency of 800 milliseconds per query. By leveraging both advanced machine learning techniques and external validation mechanisms, KorvexChecker offers a robust framework for ensuring the trustworthiness of AI-generated text, with potential applications in academia, media, and content moderation.</jats:p>
title: KorvexChecker: A BERT-Based Verification Framework for LLM Outputs in Turkish

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Verifying the complex and multi-step reasoning of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge, as holistic methods often overlook localized flaws. 
Step-by-step validation is a promising alternative, yet existing methods are often rigid. 
They struggle to adapt to diverse reasoning structures, from formal proofs to informal natural language narratives. 
To address this adaptability gap, we propose the Graph of Verification (GoV), a novel framework for adaptable and multi-granular verification. 
GoV's core innovation is its flexible node block architecture. 
This mechanism allows GoV to adaptively adjust its verification granularity—from atomic steps for formal tasks to entire paragraphs for natural language—to match the native structure of the reasoning process. 
This flexibility allows GoV to resolve the fundamental trade-off between verification precision and robustness.
Experiments on both well-structured and loosely-structured benchmarks demonstrate GoV's versatility. 
The results show that GoV's adaptive approach significantly outperforms both holistic baselines and other state-of-the-art decomposition-based methods, establishing a new standard for training-free reasoning verification.</jats:p>
title: Graph of Verification: Structured Verification of LLM Reasoning with Directed Acyclic Graphs

items.abstract: <jats:p>The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) across high-stakes domains necessitates a paradigm shift in how their truthfulness and reliability are assessed. This paper surveys the core challenges of LLM untruthfulness, specifically addressing the phenomena of hallucinations, pervasive bias, and the fundamental epistemological problem of a lack of a single ground truth. It proposes that Socratic metacognition—an integrated approach combining the introspective self-regulation of metacognition with the critical, question-based inquiry of the Socratic method—offers a robust solution. The report delineates the theoretical foundations of both human and computational metacognition, operationalizes the Socratic method for artificial intelligence (AI), and synthesizes existing architectural and conceptual frameworks. By examining models such as the Metacognitive Integrated Dual-Cycle Architecture (MIDCA) and the SocraticAI multi-agent system, a unified conceptual framework is proposed. This framework envisions a self-regulating system that uses a structured, question-based dialogue to identify and rectify its own logical inconsistencies and factual inaccuracies. The paper's contribution is a synthesis of disparate research fields, demonstrating a path toward building more reliable, transparent, and trustworthy LLMs that can navigate complex, ambiguous information spaces with a greater degree of verifiability.</jats:p>
title: A Survey on Socratic Meta-Cognition for LLM Truth Verification and related Frameworks
container-title: Journal of Advances in Developmental Research

items.abstract: Hallucination in large language model-generated summaries poses a critical safety challenge for knowledge-intensive domains such as Chinese history and culture. Existing faithfulness detection methods, primarily designed for English news summarization, treat the task as binary classification, failing to distinguish factual errors from externally verifiable unsupported additions. They also rely on large-scale annotated data and neural resources, limiting applicability in domain-specific, resource-constrained settings. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a multi-layer semantic alignment framework for hallucination safety detection in LLM-generated summaries of Chinese historical and cultural texts. The framework formalizes the task as three-way classification—Faithful, Fact Error, and Unsupported Info—and constructs an interpretable four-layer feature representation encoding lexical, syntactic, semantic, and logical correspondences between source text and summary. The framework operates without neural model dependencies, making it suitable for low-resource environments. Experiments on a newly constructed benchmark dataset of expert-verified samples spanning multiple sub-domains demonstrate that the proposed four-layer configuration substantially and consistently outperforms single-layer baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the four layers provide complementary information, with syntactic features contributing most to overall detection performance. Feature distribution analysis reveals systematic inter-class differences across all layers. This paper makes three contributions: constructing the first three-class faithfulness detection benchmark for the Chinese historical and cultural domain; proposing an interpretable multi-layer alignment feature set and validating its complementarity; and providing practical guidance for domain-specific hallucination safety detection through structured classifier comparison and feature analysis.
title: Multi-Layer Semantic Alignment for LLM Text Summarization Faithfulness Detection: A Safety Verification Framework for Chinese Historical and Cultural Domain

items.abstract: <jats:p>Biomedical Knowledge Graphs (KGs) such as PrimeKG and Hetionet offer vast structured repositories for clinical discovery; however, conventional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) suffer from black-box opacity, while standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms face catastrophic hallucinations and biological implausibility. To resolve this critical trade-off, this paper proposes BioAgent-RAG, a multi-agent orchestrated retrieval-augmented generation framework tailored for complex biomedical reasoning and transparent graph traversal. By integrating autonomous sub-agents for query decomposition, path-based KG grounding, and cross-verification, BioAgent-RAG systematically enhances biological plausibility and reduces reasoning hallucinations. Comprehensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that BioAgent-RAG substantially outperforms existing competitive baselines, RD2-KG, KGiA, and RAG-LLMs. Specifically, on the PrimeKG benchmark, it achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.952, PR-AUC of 0.814, MRR of 0.637, and superior Recall@10 and Recall@50 of 0.715 and 0.868, respectively (p &lt; 0.01). Moreover, evaluated on biological plausibility, BioAgent-RAG yields a Biomedical Factuality Score (BFS) of 0.887 on PrimeKG (0.894 on Hetionet) and a Path Reasoning Score (PRS) of 0.841 (0.862 on Hetionet), demonstrating strong preliminary correlation (0.912) with domain-expert evaluations. These findings suggest that BioAgent-RAG serves as a robust, explainable computational screening tool to prioritize drug repurposing candidates prior to in vitro validation.</jats:p>
title: BioAgent-RAG: A Knowledge-Graph-Augmented Multi-Agent LLM Framework with Self-Reflective Verification for Explainable Drug Repurposing

items.abstract: <jats:p>Formulating optimization models from natural-language specifications is a major bottleneck in engineering decision-making, because accurate translation requires both domain expertise and strict modeling discipline. Existing large language model (LLM) approaches show strong code-generation ability but often produce formulations that are executable yet semantically incorrect, or structurally invalid under solver constraints. Evolutionary Chain-of-Thought Optimization (EvoCoT) is introduced as a co-evolutionary autoformulation framework that treats model synthesis as guided discrete search over reasoning--code pairs rather than one-shot generation. EvoCoT combines three tightly coupled mechanisms: chain-of-thought evolutionary refinement for semantic exploration, memory-guided exemplar retrieval for reusing successful modeling patterns, and a co-evolving verifier that continuously acquires formulation knowledge during search and delivers dense structural-faithfulness feedback unavailable to static verifiers. Verifier feedback and retrieved successes directly regulate selection and regeneration, forming a feedback-regulated closed loop that progressively improves formulation faithfulness and solver robustness. Experiments on eight benchmark suites, including NL4OPT, MAMO, BWOR, IndustryOR, OptMATH, and ComplexOR, show consistent gains over strong zero-shot, agentic, and fine-tuned baselines, with the largest improvements on difficult industrial-scale tasks. The results demonstrate that co-evolving generation and verification is a practical pathway toward reliable, scalable, and solver-executable optimization autoformulation.</jats:p>
title: EvoCoT: Co-Evolving Generation and Verification for LLM-Based Optimization Autoformulation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Intelligent fault diagnosis and machine health management are essential for reliable operation of industrial systems, yet deploying large language models (LLMs) for these tasks introduces reliability risks including hallucinated evidence, overconfident outputs, and inconsistent reasoning. We propose CL-LLMOps, a closed-loop LLMOps framework that orchestrates LLM agents through five integrated stages—from alarm normalization to regression-tested action. At the semantic verification level—where, to our knowledge, soft computing has not previously been applied—its hierarchical mechanism combines rule-based pattern checking, cross-attention evidence scoring, and Mamdani fuzzy inference gating, jointly optimized via multi-objective particle swarm optimization, to detect hallucinations and evidence contradictions before maintenance decisions. Evaluation on three public datasets spanning power quality classification, bearing fault diagnosis, and wind turbine SCADA anomaly detection—validated across two open-source LLM backbones (Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B)—shows that CL-LLMOps achieves 98.6% diagnostic accuracy on power quality data, 99.3% on CWRU bearing data, and 95.2% on CARE wind turbine data. The framework reduces inconsistency-type hallucination from 12% to 2% relative to the fine-tuned LLM baseline while maintaining 93% action accuracy and 96% risk compliance on PQ data, with fuzzy gating specifically improving action accuracy by 5 percentage points through graded borderline handling. This work bridges LLM-powered intelligence and operational dependability for industrial deployment, offering a novel integration of established soft computing techniques—neural attention, fuzzy logic, and evolutionary optimization—at the semantic verification level for deploying trustworthy AI agents in fault diagnosis under the Industry 5.0 paradigm.</jats:p>
title: Fuzzy-Gated Verification of LLM Agents for Industrial Fault Diagnosis: An Evolutionary-Optimized Closed-Loop Framework

items.abstract: <jats:p>Gold-standard annotation is slow and expensive, and large language models (LLMs) as judges have been proposed to expedite it. Existing methods raise accuracy by sampling, asking the same question repeatedly at one evaluation pass per answer, and by deferring their least certain instances to a human. An annotation method must therefore be judged on three quantities, the accuracy attained, the evaluation passes expended, and the share of the corpus deferred to a person. This study asks whether all three can be improved by structuring the labels rather than re-examining them. The proposed method decomposes labels into a hierarchy of granularities, declares their relations as logical rules, evaluates each granularity in a mutually blind pass, and applies the rules deterministically at no model cost. It was validated on 700 building-regulation provisions for automated design compliance checking and 300 out-of-domain GoEmotions comments, against four state-of-the-art LLM-assisted annotation methods and three human experts annotating independently. On accuracy, for the regulation provisions, even a single structured pass of the proposed method reached 94.0% accuracy, above the best baseline at 89.7% and the majority verdict of three human annotators at 81.9%. At three passes, the proposed method reached its highest accuracy, 97.2%, while deferring only 9.0% of the corpus, far below the 20.0% deferral ratio of the two routing baselines. The out-of-domain corpus reproduced the pass and deferral results, with the proposed method ahead of all four baselines in paired comparisons by at least 1.7 %p at two passes, significantly so against two of them. A gold standard can therefore be built at a review load a small team can absorb.​</jats:p>
title: Structured evaluation with rule-based verification for verifiable and review-efficient LLM annotation of gold-standard datasets​

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Large language model (LLM) agents cannot guarantee that their outputs satisfy the hard business rules that govern financial transactions. We present the Verifier-Actor Neuro-Symbolic Framework (
                    <jats:sc>VA-NSF</jats:sc>
                    ), a dual-layer architecture that separates natural language understanding from formal constraint enforcement for internet finance transaction execution. A neural
                    <jats:sc>Actor</jats:sc>
                    parses financial instructions into a typed, schema-grounded abstract syntax tree (AST) through grammar-constrained decoding, and a symbolic
                    <jats:sc>Verifier</jats:sc>
                    evaluates each AST against Answer Set Programming (ASP) integrity constraints, issuing either a formal approval certificate or a structured violation report that drives targeted repair. On
                    <jats:sc>FinTxBench</jats:sc>
                    , a curated evaluation set of 8600 annotated financial instructions spanning three complexity tiers,
                    <jats:sc>VA-NSF</jats:sc>
                    attains 91.8% overall transaction accuracy (macro-averaged across the three tiers, with 94.7%, 91.2%, and 89.6% on the Simple, Compound, and Constrained tiers) at a constraint violation rate of at most 0.3%. It thereby outperforms four LLM baselines by 13 to 51 percentage points and reduces violations 30-fold, all within a median latency of 399 ms, of which ASP verification accounts for only 24 ms. Ablations confirm that each component contributes independently, and cross-domain experiments on payment processing, procurement, payroll, and inventory modules show at most 5.8 percentage points of degradation. All formal guarantees are relative to the fidelity of the encoded rule set, and the evaluation uses a curated benchmark with up to 80 rules; we therefore discuss explicitly the resulting limitations regarding noisy real-world language, rule-set scale, and human-escalation overhead.
                  </jats:p>
title: Neuro-symbolic constraint verification for LLM-driven internet finance transaction execution

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into the hardware design verification (DV) landscape represents a pivotal moment in the evolution of verification workflows. LLMs offer powerful capabilities for natural language processing, code generation, and collaborative assistance, allowing them to bridge gaps between code comprehension, coverage analysis, and team communication. This review synthesizes the most recent developments in LLM-driven DV, covering assertion generation, coverage diagnostics, and UVM testbench completion. We propose an architectural model where modular LLM agents act as code analyzers, coverage interpreters, and assertion suggesters, working alongside human engineers. Experimental findings show clear advantages in accuracy, interpretability, and engineering efficiency. We conclude with an analysis of emerging trends and the necessary steps to industrialize LLM adoption in formal verification.</jats:p>
title: LLM-driven verification assistance: Bridging code, coverage and collaboration

<jats:p>Language model agents increasingly propose actions, observe external feedback, and explain their own behavior. Their confidence and rationales are convenient oversight signals, but convenience is not verification. We introduce an environment-grounded audit in which every intermediate proposal receives an exact outcome. A language model operates an evolutionary Contexto search whosefeedback function assigns every valid guess an exact rank without human annotation. Across 200 runs spanning five configurations and three model families, four reporting configurations produce 12,249 self-reports. We test three assumptions: stated confidence is calibrated, inherited rationales affect later proposals, and outcome-based selection improves report quality. All three fail. Operators overstate top-100 success by factors of 4.8 to 9.3, while calibration and discrimination dissociate across model families. Controlled interventions on 754 inherited rationales bound any measured benefit of the genuine rationale to roughly 250 ranks. Neither fitness-based nor random selection produces a detectable selection differential or parent-to-offspring transmission in report accuracy, despite sharply different search behavior. Agent self-reports should therefore be treated as claims to verify against the environment, not as evidence of their own reliability.
Lab: Machine Intelligence and Biocomputing Lab (MIB) at School of Computing
Supervisor: Dr. Ting Hu
Supporting lab supervisor: Ryan Zhou</jats:p>
title: Self-Reports Are Not Verification
